In many cases, the executive will effectively have the last word on 
statutory interpretation either because the administrative decision at issue 
is simply obscure from public view or because it would be difficult to 
identify a plaintiff harmed or threatened with harm of sufficient 
particularity to meet the Supreme Court’s requirements for standing to 
sue. The concepts of standing and nonreviewability are explored in detail 
in Chapter 7.
Because of the “last word” phenomenon, the role of government 
attorneys as potentially the ultimate interpreters of law is profoundly 
important, arguably imposing special ethical obligations on government 
attorneys in their advisory role:
The quality of [government lawyering] is essential because, for the

For this reason, it is also essential that government lawyers 
understand their unique roles as both advisers and advocates. In 
adversarial proceedings before courts of law, it may be fine for 
each of two contesting sides, including the government, to have a 
zealous, and not wholly impartial defense, while the judge acts as 
a neutral decision maker. But government lawyers, in their 
advisory function, must themselves play a more objective, even 
quasi-adjudicative role. They must give the law their most 
conscientious interpretation. If they do not, there will frequently 
be no one else effectively situated to do the job of assuring 
dihgence in legal compliance.
